title: In a spherical head model at the thermal-noise and ultrasound safety limits, scalp acoustoelectric imaging needs minutes to days per 4-mm voxel to detect evoked cortical currents
abstract: Scalp acoustoelectric brain imaging needs minutes to days of averaging for each 4-mm voxel to detect evoked cortical currents, even with ideal electrodes at the thermal-noise limit and within ultrasound safety limits. This is important because groups develop this method as a noninvasive way to map brain currents with millimeter and millisecond resolution. In the method, focused ultrasound changes the electrical resistivity of tissue by a small fraction (the acoustoelectric constant, about 0.04% per MPa), and scalp electrodes record a megahertz voltage from the neural current in the focus. We calculated the best possible signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) with a four-shell spherical head, the optimal combination of all scalp electrodes, thermal (Johnson) noise, and the mechanical-index, FDA-intensity and ITRUSST thermal-index limits. We checked the formulas against a full focused-field calculation and an independent head-model solution. The signal depends on the current dipole moment density q, which is the dipole moment per area of active cortex. At 0.5 MHz, a cortical patch gives the signal of a point current of about 30 microamperes for each nA m/mm2 of q. Thus published phantom detection thresholds (360 to 580 microamperes) are 7 to 235 times above real activity (q from 0.1 to 2). If only the extracellular fluid is modulated (an upper bound), SNR = 3 needs about 10 min when q = 1 and 32 h when q = 0.1, and a map of 100 voxels needs 1.4 days to 4 months. Heating of the skull, where the converging beam is about 1 cm wide, sets the intensity. Neural currents form closed loops, so the modulation inside cells can cancel part of the signal; if 70% cancels, the times are 11 to 22 times longer. A published live-heart measurement agrees with the upper-bound model within a factor of 3. Cortex whose normal is more than about 15 degrees outside the beam aperture gives only edge signals. An implanted contact 5 mm from the voxel makes the times 100 to 180 times shorter. Thus noninvasive acoustoelectric imaging cannot map typical brain activity, but recording near implanted contacts is practical. Main limits: a spherical head; acoustoelectric constants from saline and heart only; and one phantom study with injected currents that, taken at face value, implies times up to 80 times shorter, but does not report all acquisition parameters.
